text: A deep fake is defined as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities, or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful [1]. This definition applies to content used for purposes such as generating or manipulating text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest [2].

The Act defines AI literacy as the skills, knowledge, and understanding that enable providers, deployers, and affected persons to make informed decisions about deploying AI systems while recognizing the opportunities and risks involved [1]. This obligation requires providers and deployers to support staff and other personnel in developing this literacy, though it does not mandate that they guarantee a specific level of literacy for any individual [2]. The Commission and Member States are tasked with supporting providers and SMEs in fulfilling this obligation by publishing practical examples on a single information platform [2]. Additionally, the Board may adopt recommendations to assist the Commission and Member States in promoting AI literacy, including by setting common objectives [3].

A small mid-cap enterprise (SMC) is defined in Article 3 of the Regulation as a small mid-cap enterprise as defined in point (14b) of the Annex to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 [1]. This definition is used to support innovation and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence [3]. The Act specifically mentions micro- and small enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC when discussing administrative burdens [4].

A change to an AI system is a "substantial modification" if it occurs after the system has been placed on the market or put into service and is not foreseen or planned in the initial conformity assessment [1]. This applies to high-risk AI systems that undergo a new conformity assessment procedure [2]. Additionally, any modification that results in a change to the intended purpose of an AI system [3] constitutes a substantial modification.

The AI Office is the Commission's function of contributing to the implementation, monitoring, and supervision of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, as well as AI governance [1]. It is responsible for developing Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office [3]. The AI Office may also assist in the assessment of available standards and encourage the review and adaptation of codes of practice [2].

The AI Act does not apply to AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities [1]. This exclusion applies to systems placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification for such purposes [1]. Additionally, the Act does not apply to AI systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used exclusively for these purposes [1]. The Act also excludes AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development [2].

AI systems released under free and open-source licences are exempt from the regulation unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50 [1]. This exemption applies to providers of general-purpose AI models that allow for access, usage, modification, and distribution of the model, provided that parameters, weights, architecture, and usage information are publicly available [2][3]. However, this exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risks [3]. Additionally, the regulation does not apply to third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes, or components under a free and open-source licence, except for general-purpose AI models [4].

No, an AI model built solely for scientific research and development is not covered by this Regulation, as it is explicitly excluded from the scope of the Act [1]. This exclusion applies to AI systems or models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development [1]. Consequently, such activities must instead be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law [2].

The AI Act applies to your company because you are a provider or importer of AI systems whose output is used in the EU, regardless of your location [4]. However, the Act does not apply to your company if your AI systems were specifically developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development purposes [5].

Companies must take measures to support the development of AI literacy for their staff and other persons dealing with AI systems, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education, and training [1]. This obligation does not require companies to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy for any individual [1]. The Commission and Member States shall support and facilitate efforts to fulfill this obligation, particularly for SMEs [1]. The Board may adopt recommendations to support the Commission in promoting AI literacy, including by setting out common objectives [3].

Natural persons assigned human oversight to high-risk AI systems must be enabled to understand the system's capacities and limitations, monitor its operation, and detect anomalies or dysfunctions [2]. They should also remain aware of the tendency to over-rely on automated outputs, including the possibility of automation bias [2]. Furthermore, these individuals must be able to decide not to use the system, override its output, or reverse it in any particular situation [2]. Additionally, they should have the ability to intervene in the system's operation or use a 'stop' button to halt it in a safe state [2].

The provider must keep the EU declaration of conformity for a period of 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [1][4]. This requirement applies to the provider and their authorised representative, who must provide a copy of the declaration to competent authorities upon request [1][5]. Additionally, importers must retain a copy of the declaration for 10 years following the system's placement on the market [2].

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, the provider or their authorised representative must register it in the EU database [1]. Public authorities and persons acting on their behalf must also register the system and its use [3]. Systems that are not high-risk do not require registration under these specific provisions [2].

Yes, as an employer, you must inform your workers' representatives and affected workers before putting a high-risk AI system into service or use at the workplace [1]. This information must be provided in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on information of workers and their representatives [1]. The high-risk AI systems you are referring to include those intended for recruitment, selection, or decisions affecting work-related relationships [2].

Deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to deploying high-risk AI systems [5]. Additionally, deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use in areas listed in Annex III must also conduct such an assessment [5]. The AI Office may provide a template to facilitate compliance with these obligations [5].

The fundamental rights impact assessment must include the measures to be taken in the case of the materialisation of risks, such as internal governance and complaint mechanisms [3]. It also requires the identification of the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by the system's use [4]. Additionally, the assessment must cover the possibility of cross-referencing or including relevant parts of a data protection impact assessment [1].

Yes, deployers of high-risk AI systems must inform natural persons that they are subject to the use of such systems when making decisions or assisting in those decisions [1]. This obligation applies to systems used for employment, workers' management, and access to self-employment, including recruitment, job advertisements, and performance monitoring [2]. Additionally, if the AI system produces legal effects or significantly affects an individual's health, safety, or fundamental rights, the person has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the system's role and the decision's main elements [4].

If a provider determines that an AI system listed in Annex III is not high-risk, it must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service [1]. The provider is also subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2) and must provide the documentation of the assessment upon request from national competent authorities [1]. If the market surveillance authority later finds that the system is high-risk, the provider must take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance with the Regulation's requirements [2]. Additionally, the provider must ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all AI systems it has made available on the Union market [5].

Yes, SMEs may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner, provided they do not have partner enterprises or linked enterprises [1]. This simplified approach applies to micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises as defined in the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC [2]. However, this exemption does not apply to high-risk AI systems or other obligations such as Articles 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 72, and 73 [1].

Your employer cannot use AI to infer your emotions at work unless the use is intended for medical or safety reasons [1]. Employers must inform workers' representatives and affected workers before deploying such high-risk AI systems [2]. This prohibition applies to all areas of employment, including recruitment and performance monitoring [5].

Yes, the use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics is prohibited under the Act. This ban specifically covers practices where such social scoring leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment of individuals in social contexts unrelated to the data's origin [1]. Additionally, the Act prohibits the use of AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities related to age, disability, or specific social/economic situations to distort behaviour and cause harm [2].

No, it is prohibited to place on the market, put into service, or use AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage [1]. This prohibition applies to all activities involving such systems, including their placement on the market or use [1].

The ban on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery applies from the date of the Act's entry into force, which is 27 July 2026. This prohibition covers the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic images of an identifiable natural person's intimate parts without their consent [1]. The ban applies to all such practices, including those that do not increase exposure or alter the nature of the activities [2].

Yes, police may use real-time facial recognition in public spaces, but only for specific law enforcement objectives and under strict conditions. This use must be limited to confirming the identity of a specifically targeted individual [1][3]. Such systems must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards, including a fundamental rights impact assessment and registration in the EU database [2]. However, in cases of duly justified urgency, the system may be commenced without prior registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay [2]. Additionally, the use must be notified to relevant authorities and comply with national rules regarding data protection [5].
If the police start using a real-time remote biometric identification system in an emergency without prior authorisation, they must request it within 24 hours. [1]

Under the new AI Act, an AI system that manipulates an identifiable natural person's intimate parts without increasing their exposure is prohibited, even if the manipulation does not alter the nature of the activity [1][2]. This prohibition applies to the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of such an AI system [2]. The ban covers scenarios where the generation or manipulation is the intended purpose of the system or is reasonably foreseeable and reproducible without significant technical safeguards [3].

An AI system is considered high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product or is itself a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and the product requires a third-party conformity assessment for its safety component [1]. Additionally, AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk regardless of their specific use [4].

An AI system listed in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, provided it meets specific conditions such as performing a narrow procedural task or improving a previously completed human activity [1]. This classification applies where the system is intended to detect decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment or performing profiling [1]. The Commission may also amend the list by removing systems that no longer pose significant risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights [2].

AI tools that detect cheating during exams are not classified as high-risk systems because they perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to the use cases listed in Annex III, rather than replacing or influencing human assessment [1]. Consequently, they do not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons [1].

No, software that only organises the logistics of a political campaign is not a high-risk AI system because it does not fall under the specific areas listed in Annex III, Section 8(a) of the Act. The Act explicitly excludes such tools from the definition of high-risk systems, stating that they are not intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons. [1]

Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs for a period of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise [1]. Financial institutions subject to specific internal governance requirements must maintain these logs as part of their documentation under relevant Union financial services law [1][2]. Additionally, providers must retain the technical documentation and EU declaration of conformity for a period ending 10 years after the system is placed on the market [3][4][5].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep logs for a period of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise [1][2]. This requirement applies to logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system [2]. Financial institutions subject to specific internal governance requirements must maintain these logs as part of their documentation under relevant Union financial services law [1][2].

The provider must report a serious incident immediately after establishing a causal link or reasonable likelihood of such a link, with a deadline of 15 days in general cases [1]. If the incident involves the death of a person, the report must be provided within 10 days [2]. In cases of widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3, point (49)(b), the report must be provided within two days [4]. Additionally, the provider must perform necessary investigations and corrective actions without delay following the report [3].

The reporting deadline for a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system that results in death is 10 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the incident. This requirement applies specifically when the provider or deployer establishes, or as soon as it suspects, a causal relationship between the high-risk AI system and the death [1].

Yes, providers must ensure that AI systems interacting directly with natural persons are designed so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless the interaction is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person [1]. This transparency obligation applies to all AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons [1].

You must disclose that your deepfake video has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation applies to all deep fakes unless the content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work, in which case the transparency obligations are limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. Satire is explicitly treated differently, as the transparency obligations for such content are limited rather than fully requiring disclosure.

Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up, keep up-to-date, and make available information and documentation to AI system providers, which includes elements set out in Annex XII [1]. They are also required to draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation containing specific information set out in Annex XI [2]. Additionally, providers must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and national competent authorities [3]. Furthermore, they must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights [4]. Finally, providers must draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training of the model [5].

The Commission may consider several criteria to determine if a general-purpose AI model has systemic risk, including the number of registered end-users [1], the quality or size of the data set [2], the number of parameters of the model [3], the benchmarks and evaluations of its capabilities [4], and the input and output modalities [5].
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have a high impact on the internal market if it has been made available to at least 10,000 registered business users established in the Union [1].

Yes, providers of general-purpose AI models must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, specifically to identify and comply with a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [1]. This obligation applies to all providers of general-purpose AI models [1].

The maximum fines for SMEs and start-ups are determined by the lower of the percentages or amounts specified in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 of Article 99 [1]. Paragraph 6 states that for SMEs, the fine is up to the lower of these percentages or amounts [1]. Paragraph 6a clarifies that for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMCs), the fine is also up to the lower of the percentages or amounts specified in paragraphs 4 and 5 [5]. Since the Act does not explicitly distinguish between "SMEs" and "start-ups" in the penalty calculation, the rules apply uniformly to both categories based on the lower percentage or amount [1][5].

The AI Act does not provide any specific relief for small mid-cap companies. Fines for providers of general-purpose AI models are capped at 3% of their annual worldwide turnover or EUR 15,000,000, whichever is higher [5]. Administrative fines for non-compliance with AI system requirements are capped at EUR 750,000 [1]. Fines for non-compliance with prohibitions on AI practices are capped at EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher [2]. There is no mention of exemptions or reduced liability for small or mid-sized enterprises in the provided passages.

You have the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations from the deployer regarding the role of the AI system and the main elements of the loan decision [2]. This right applies to high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III that produce legal effects or significantly affect your health, safety, or fundamental rights [2]. However, this right does not apply if the use of the AI system is covered by exceptions or restrictions provided by Union or national law in compliance with Union law [2]. You must also ensure that this right is not otherwise provided for under Union law [2].

Each EU Member State must establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at its national level by 2 August 2027. This deadline applies to all Member States, though the obligation can be fulfilled by participating in an existing sandbox if that participation provides equivalent national coverage [1]. The Commission may also provide technical support, advice, and tools for the establishment and operation of these sandboxes [1].

The high-risk requirements apply to AI systems listed in Annex III [1][2][3][4][5]. These systems must comply with the requirements set out in Section 2 [1][2][3][4][5]. The provider must opt for specific conformity assessment procedures based on the standards applied [1][2][3][4][5]. If harmonised standards or common specifications are not available, the provider must use internal control or a notified body [3][5].

The high-risk rules for AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I apply from the date of the notification procedure in accordance with the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. This date is evidenced through the assessment as part of the existing notification [2].

The AI Act applies from 2 August 2026, except for specific chapters that apply earlier or later [5]. High-risk AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply by 2 August 2030 if they undergo significant design changes [1]. General-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027 [3]. AI systems that are components of large-scale IT systems established by legal acts listed in Annex X must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030 [4].

High-risk AI systems placed on the market before the date of application of Chapter III shall not be subject to the new high-risk rules unless they undergo significant changes in their designs. The Regulation applies to such systems only if, as from that date, they are subject to significant changes in their designs [1]. Providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities must take necessary steps to comply with the requirements by 2 August 2030 [1].

The Act defines a **provider** as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that uses an AI system under its authority [1]. A **deployer** is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that uses an AI system under its authority, except where the system is used in a personal non-professional activity [1]. The key difference lies in the specific context of use: a provider uses the system under its authority, whereas a deployer uses it in the course of a personal non-professional activity [1].

The maximum fine for non-compliance with prohibited AI practices is up to EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whereas the fine for breaching a deployer's obligations under high-risk AI systems is up to EUR 750,000 [1][3].

The Act does not specify a monetary cost for registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database. Registration is a mandatory administrative requirement for deployers and providers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III [1][2]. The EU database must contain personal data only insofar as necessary for collecting and processing information [5]. Access to restricted sections of the database is limited to the Commission and national authorities [3].

The AI Act does not provide any tax incentives for AI start-ups. The Act focuses on regulatory measures such as access to AI regulatory sandboxes, awareness raising, and standardisation support [1][2][3][4][5]. It does not mention any financial tax benefits or deductions for companies developing artificial intelligence systems.

The AI Act does not set a minimum wage for data annotators. The Act focuses on data governance and the prohibition of prohibited AI practices, but it does not contain provisions regarding labor standards or minimum wages for individuals involved in data annotation [1][3].

The AI Act does not contain any information regarding the United Kingdom's implementation timeline. The Act applies only to the European Union and does not address the United Kingdom. The AI Act passages provided do not answer this question.
